title: HE TASTED A LITTLE HONEY… AND HIS OWN FATHER SENTENCED HIM TO DIE.
paragraphs: HE TASTED A LITTLE HONEY… AND HIS OWN FATHER SENTENCED HIM TO DIE.

The terrifying story of a king’s reckless oath, a son who unknowingly broke it, and an entire army that refused to let a foolish command destroy the man God had used to deliver them. — 1 Samuel 14:24–45
He was fighting for his father's kingdom. He was risking his life for God's people. He was exhausted, hungry, and standing in the middle of a battlefield.
Then he saw honey.
Just a little honey.
He reached out his staff, tasted it, and felt strength return to his body.
He had no idea that his father had already spoken words that could cost him his life.
And when the truth finally came out, the king was prepared to watch his own son die.
Not because the young man had betrayed Israel.
Not because he had abandoned God.
Not because he had deliberately rebelled.
But because he had eaten something he did not even know was forbidden.
And the most disturbing part?
The father who condemned him was the very king who should have been protecting him.
This is not a story about honey.

It is a story about what happens when spiritual authority becomes entangled with pride, when religious words are spoken without wisdom, and when the people closest to us become casualties of our need to be right.
But buried inside this ancient battlefield is another truth.
One that reaches beyond Jonathan, beyond Saul, beyond Israel.
A truth that leads us straight to Jesus Christ.
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing in a person's life is not an enemy standing in front of them.
Sometimes it is a voice they have been taught never to question.
And sometimes the first step toward freedom is discovering that God's authority and human authority are not always saying the same thing.
The battle had already begun.
Israel was fighting the Philistines, a powerful enemy that had long threatened God's people.
King Saul occupied the throne, but something remarkable had happened before the incident with the honey.
His son Jonathan had taken a courageous step of faith.
With only his armor-bearer beside him, Jonathan approached a Philistine outpost.
He was not leading an army.
He did not have overwhelming numbers.
He did not possess the kind of military advantage that would make victory appear inevitable.
But he believed something about God that many people forget when circumstances become terrifying.
Jonathan said:
“For there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.” — 1 Samuel 14:6, KJV
Think about that.
Two men.
An enemy position.
Almost impossible odds.
And a young man who understood that God's ability to deliver His people was not determined by the size of their army.
Jonathan and his armor-bearer attacked, and the Lord brought confusion upon the Philistine forces.
Panic spread.
The enemy began turning against itself.
Israel's opportunity for victory was unfolding.
God was doing something extraordinary.
And then Saul made a decision that would nearly turn a day of deliverance into a family tragedy.
First Samuel 14:24 records:
“And the men of Israel were distressed that day: for Saul had adjured the people, saying, Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening, that I may be avenged on mine enemies.” — KJV
Read those words carefully.
Not merely the prohibition.
The motive.
“That I may be avenged on mine enemies.”
Saul had placed the soldiers under an oath not to eat until evening.
They were fighting.
Marching.
Pursuing.
Bleeding.
Exhausting themselves in battle.
Yet they were forbidden to take nourishment.
And Saul connected that prohibition to his desire for vengeance.
The Hebrew text gives us an important detail.
The word translated “adjured” is הִשְׁבִּיעַ (hishbiaʿ), a form of the verb שָׁבַע (shavaʿ), meaning to cause someone to swear or bind them by an oath.
This was not simply a father's preference or a king's casual suggestion.
Saul had imposed a solemn obligation upon the people.
And the oath carried a curse.
But solemn language does not automatically make a decision wise.
Invoking God's name does not automatically make someone's motives holy.
And holding authority does not make every command an accurate reflection of God's heart.
Saul's soldiers were already weary.
The narrative tells us they entered a wooded area where honey was available.
Imagine what that must have felt like.
Their bodies were crying out for strength.
Food was right in front of them.
Yet no one dared touch it.
First Samuel 14:26 says:
“And when the people were come into the wood, behold, the honey dropped; but no man put his hand to his mouth: for the people feared the oath.” — KJV
The honey was there.
The hunger was real.
But fear restrained them.
Then Jonathan arrived.
He had not heard his father's command.
He had been away when Saul placed the army under the oath.
He did not know.
And Scripture is explicit about that.

“But Jonathan heard not when his father charged the people with the oath: wherefore he put forth the end of the rod that was in his hand, and dipped it in an honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth; and his eyes were enlightened.” — 1 Samuel 14:27, KJV
His eyes were enlightened.
The Hebrew expression is וַתָּאֹרְנָה עֵינָיו (vattāʾornāh ʿênāyw).
Literally, the language conveys that his eyes became bright.
In the context, it describes the visible restoration of a weary man after receiving nourishment.
The text is not teaching that honey gave Jonathan supernatural revelation.
It is describing renewed physical vitality.
He was exhausted.
He ate.
His strength began to return.
That is all.
And yet that ordinary human act had placed him in conflict with an extraordinary royal oath.
Someone in the army told him what his father had commanded.
And Jonathan's response was astonishing.
He did not praise the restriction.
He did not pretend that exhaustion was holiness.
He did not call an unwise decision righteous merely because a king had made it.
He said:
“My father hath troubled the land.” — 1 Samuel 14:29, KJV
Then he pointed to the evidence.
His own eyes had brightened after tasting a little honey.
And he reasoned that if the soldiers had been permitted to eat from the enemy's provisions, their victory could have been greater.
Jonathan was not dismissing God's commandments.
He was recognizing the destructive consequences of his father's decision.
There is a difference.
And that difference matters.
Because some people have spent years confusing loyalty to God with unquestioning submission to every human demand made in God's name.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
You were told that asking questions meant you lacked faith.
You were told that expressing pain meant you were rebellious.
You were told that setting a healthy boundary meant you were dishonoring someone.
You were told to remain silent because the person hurting you carried a title.
Father.
Mother.
Pastor.
Leader.
Mentor.
Someone respected.
Someone powerful.
Someone who knew how to speak about God.
And because you loved God, you assumed that resisting their behavior meant resisting Him.
But listen carefully.
Respecting authority does not require pretending that authority can never be wrong.
Scripture commands honor, humility, and proper submission. It also teaches that human authority is accountable to God.
The apostles themselves declared:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29, KJV
That does not give us permission to become arrogant, lawless, or contemptuous.
It reminds us that no human being occupies the throne that belongs to the Lord.
Not a king.
Not a parent.
Not a religious leader.
Not even someone who genuinely believes their intentions are good.
And Saul's story becomes even more disturbing.
Because the damage did not end with the hungry soldiers.
After the battle, the exhausted people rushed upon the spoil and ate meat with the blood still in it, violating God's command concerning blood.
First Samuel 14:32–33 records their wrongdoing.
This is important.
Saul's oath did not make the people innocent of their subsequent sin.
They remained responsible for obeying God's law.
But his restriction had contributed to the desperate conditions in which that sin occurred.
An attempt to enforce one religiously framed command had helped create circumstances in which the people broke an actual divine command.
There is a warning here for every believer entrusted with influence.
When our rules become more important than God's revealed will, we can end up burdening the very people we claim to be helping.
Jesus confronted religious leaders who behaved this way.
He said:
“For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.” — Matthew 23:4, KJV
Christ was not condemning genuine obedience.
He was exposing religious hypocrisy and oppressive leadership.
There is a kind of spirituality that loves control more than compassion.
A kind of leadership that demands sacrifice from others while refusing to examine its own heart.
A kind of righteousness that can quote commandments but has forgotten mercy.
And if we are not careful, we can become that kind of person.
Not only in churches.
In our homes.
In our marriages.
In our friendships.
In the way we raise our children.
In the way we respond when someone challenges us.
We can become so committed to proving that we were right that we stop asking whether we have wounded someone we love.
And then comes the moment that makes this account almost unbearable.
Saul sought divine guidance about continuing the pursuit of the Philistines, but God gave him no answer that day.
Saul concluded that sin must be present and initiated a process to identify the offender.
He declared that even if the guilt were found in Jonathan, his own son, Jonathan would surely die.
The lot eventually identified Jonathan.
Saul confronted him.
Jonathan admitted what he had done.
He had tasted a little honey.
He had not known about the oath when he ate.
Yet Saul responded:
“God do so and more also: for thou shalt surely die, Jonathan.” — 1 Samuel 14:44, KJV
Stop there.
A father.
Looking at his son.
The son whose courage had helped bring deliverance to Israel.
The son who had acted in faith when the odds were overwhelming.
The son who had unknowingly violated a command issued in his absence.
And the father was prepared to put him to death.
Why?
The narrative does not give us access to every private thought in Saul's heart.
We should not pretend that it does.
But it does show a king determined to uphold his oath even when the circumstances revealed the terrible consequences of doing so.
And it forces us to confront a painful possibility.
A person can become so determined to defend a decision that they lose sight of the human being suffering because of it.
Have you ever watched someone choose their pride over reconciliation?
Have you ever waited for an apology that never came?
Have you ever heard someone defend their intentions while refusing to acknowledge the damage they caused?
Perhaps you were the one waiting.
Perhaps you were the one who caused the wound.
Perhaps you are still carrying the consequences of words spoken in anger years ago.
Words that were never taken back.
Words that changed the atmosphere of a home.
Words that made a child afraid to speak.
Words that taught someone to hide their mistakes rather than seek help.
And perhaps the hardest part was that the person who spoke them believed they were doing what was right.
Saul's story warns us that religious seriousness is not the same thing as spiritual maturity.
A vow can be solemn and still be rash.
A decision can be forceful and still be foolish.
A leader can possess authority and still need correction.
And a father can love the idea of being obeyed more than he demonstrates the wisdom required to lead.
But the story does not end with Jonathan's death.
Because Jonathan did not die.
Something extraordinary happened.
The people intervened.
They had witnessed what God had done through Jonathan.
They refused to accept that the man who had been instrumental in Israel's deliverance should be executed for this offense.
Listen to their words:

“Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the LORD liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day.” — 1 Samuel 14:45, KJV
And then Scripture says:
“So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not.”
The Hebrew verb translated “rescued” is וַיִּפְדּוּ (vayyifdû), from the root פָּדָה (padah), meaning to ransom, redeem, or deliver.
In this context, the people secured Jonathan's release from the threatened execution.
The word is powerful.
But we must handle it faithfully.
The passage does not describe a payment made for Jonathan's life, nor does it explicitly identify Jonathan as a prophetic symbol of Jesus.
It tells us that the people intervened and he was spared.
That is the historical meaning.
And it is already remarkable.
The king had pronounced death.
The people recognized the injustice of carrying out that sentence.
And Jonathan lived.
But there is something else we need to understand.
The people did not save Jonathan by declaring that God's holiness no longer mattered.
They appealed to the evidence of God's work through him.
They recognized that the king's rash oath must not be treated as though it were the final expression of God's will.
And that distinction is essential.
Because the Bible does not teach that every vow should be carried out regardless of whether fulfilling it would require evil.
God does not become obligated to approve sin simply because someone has sworn an oath.
The Lord calls His people to truthfulness, reverence, and obedience—not to defending destructive decisions at any cost.
And now the story turns toward us.
Because perhaps you have never stood on an ancient battlefield.
Perhaps you have never tasted honey from the end of a wooden staff.
Perhaps no king has ever pronounced a death sentence over your life.
But you know what it means to live beneath words that feel impossible to escape.
“You will never amount to anything.”
“You always disappoint me.”
“God could never use someone like you.”
“You have ruined everything.”
“You are too far gone.”
“You should be ashamed of yourself.”
Some of those words may have come from other people.
Some may have come from your own mouth.
And some may have become so familiar that you mistake them for God's voice.
But not every accusation is the voice of conviction.
Not every burden comes from the Holy Spirit.
Not every person who speaks with certainty is speaking truth.
God's Word must be our standard.
And His Word tells us something astonishing about those who belong to Jesus Christ.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
No condemnation.
That does not mean no correction.
It does not mean no consequences.
It does not mean sin is harmless.
It means that those who are united to Christ by faith are no longer under the judicial condemnation their sins deserve.
And that is not because God decided that sin did not matter.
It is because Jesus Christ bore the judgment sinners could never bear for themselves.
Here is where we must be careful with the comparison.
Jonathan was a courageous man who unknowingly violated his father's oath.
Jesus Christ was the perfectly righteous Son who knowingly and willingly obeyed His Father's saving purpose.
Jonathan was spared from death.
Jesus voluntarily entered death.
Jonathan's deliverance came through the intervention of the people.
Our redemption comes through the sacrifice of the Son of God.
The stories are not identical.
And we do not need to force them to be.
The contrast is enough to make us tremble.
Saul was willing to see his son die because of a rash human oath.
But the heavenly Father sent His Son in perfect wisdom and love to save people who truly were guilty of sin.
And Jesus was not a helpless victim of a Father's uncontrolled anger.
He willingly gave Himself.
Christ said:
“Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.” — John 10:17–18, KJV
Do you see the difference?
Jonathan did not know the command that threatened him.
Jesus knew exactly what obedience would cost.
Jonathan tasted honey and regained his strength.
Jesus tasted death so that sinners might receive eternal life.
Jonathan was rescued from execution.
Jesus was crucified, buried, and raised from the dead.
And because He lives, everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
The New Testament declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor and gracious generosity.
In Ephesians, salvation is presented as God's gift, not something human beings can earn through their own achievements.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot suffer enough to make yourself worthy.
You cannot undo yesterday by pretending it never happened.
You cannot save yourself by being more religious than everyone around you.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Maybe that is the part you have been resisting.
You have spent so long trying to prove you are strong that you have forgotten how to surrender.
You have learned to smile while carrying shame.
You know how to quote Scripture while hiding a broken heart.
You know how to attend church while avoiding the conversation you need to have with God.
You have become skilled at looking spiritually alive while privately feeling exhausted.
And now, somewhere inside you, there is a question you are afraid to ask.
What if I have been trying to earn what Jesus already offers by grace?
Listen.
God's grace does not excuse your sin.
It calls you out of it.
The cross does not tell you that your rebellion was harmless.
It tells you that your rebellion was so serious that redemption required the death of Christ.
But it also tells you that God's mercy is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can turn away from what is destroying you.
You can seek forgiveness from those you have wounded.
You can begin walking in obedience even if the consequences of yesterday have not disappeared.
And when you fall, you do not need to hide from the only Savior who can restore you.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
That promise is not an invitation to remain comfortable in darkness.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something else.
If you have used your authority to wound someone, do not hide behind your position.
If you are a parent who has crushed your child's spirit with careless words, humility is not weakness.
If you are a husband or wife who has demanded respect while withholding tenderness, repentance is not humiliation.
If you are a Christian leader who has confused personal preference with biblical command, admitting that you were wrong does not dishonor God.
It honors the truth.
You do not have to keep defending a harmful decision simply because you made it.
You can stop.
You can acknowledge the damage.
You can ask forgiveness without demanding immediate trust.
You can begin demonstrating change through patient, consistent obedience.
And if you are the one who has been wounded, remember this:
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
It does not require you to remain in danger.
Reconciliation and restored trust may require repentance, accountability, and time.
The Gospel calls us to mercy and truth together.
Jesus never asks us to replace one with the other.
And perhaps that is why this story is so unforgettable.
Because the honey was never the real danger.
The greater danger was a king whose judgment had become entangled with his own words.
Jonathan needed nourishment.
Saul needed wisdom.
The army needed deliverance.
And the entire situation exposed how quickly human pride can complicate what God is doing.
Now consider the question that reaches into every home, every church, every relationship, and every human heart.
Are you more committed to defending your words, or to obeying God's Word?
Because there may be someone waiting for you to admit that you were wrong.
There may be a relationship suffering because you refuse to apologize.
There may be a child who needs your compassion more than another lecture.
There may be a believer who needs sound biblical counsel rather than another burden.
There may be a wounded person who has begun to believe that God is as harsh and unpredictable as the people who misrepresented Him.
And there may be someone reading this who has never truly surrendered to Jesus Christ.
You have admired Him.
You have heard about Him.
You have shared Christian posts.
You have said prayers.
But deep inside, you know you have been keeping Him at a distance.
If that is you, do not confuse religious familiarity with saving faith.
Christ does not merely invite you to appreciate His teachings.
He calls you to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
You do not need to make yourself perfect before coming.
You need to come to the One who alone can forgive and transform you.
Tell Him the truth.
Tell Him about the sin you have excused.
The bitterness you have protected.
The pride you have disguised.
The wounds you have hidden.
The fear that has kept you silent.
The exhaustion beneath your religious appearance.
And ask Him for mercy.
Not because a prayer formula has magical power.
But because Jesus Christ is the risen Savior who receives those who come to Him in faith.
If you do not know what to say, you can begin here:

Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to obey Your Word, to walk in truth, and to love what You love. I surrender my life to You. Amen.
And if you have been following Christ for years, perhaps your prayer is different.
Perhaps you need to ask Him to show you where pride has replaced humility.
Where control has replaced love.
Where fear has replaced trust.
Where you have made your own expectations heavier than the burdens God actually calls people to carry.
Do not merely admire Jonathan's courage.
Ask God to give you courage to obey Him.
Do not merely condemn Saul's foolishness.
Ask God to expose the foolishness that may still be hiding in you.
And do not merely celebrate that Jonathan was rescued.
Remember the greater redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest need of humanity is not simply to escape harsh people, broken systems, or painful memories.
Our deepest need is to be reconciled to the holy God against whom we have sinned.
And that reconciliation is found in Christ alone.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn spiritual pain into entertainment.
But to keep bringing people back to Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
Some people will encounter a biblical truth through an article on their phone long before they are willing to walk into a church.
Some are believers who have become discouraged.
Some are searching for answers.
Some are quietly battling temptation.
Some are trying to rebuild their lives after terrible decisions.
Some have almost stopped praying.
And some are one honest encounter with the Gospel away from realizing that the door of mercy is still open.
That is why sharing matters.
If this message made you think of someone, consider sending it to them privately with love rather than using it to shame them.
You never know who may be silently asking God for clarity while appearing perfectly fine to everyone else.
And if this story has exposed something in your own heart, I want to invite you into a genuine conversation.
You do not need to reveal private details publicly.
Sometimes the beginning of healing is simply being honest enough to ask for prayer.
Your words may encourage someone who feels too ashamed to believe that change is possible.
And if you believe this ministry is helping people encounter the truth of God's Word, there is another meaningful way to participate.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It is not proof that you love Jesus more than someone who cannot afford to give.
And it should never replace your responsibility to support your local church, care for your family, or practice wise stewardship.
The principle is beautifully expressed in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That is the heart behind the invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But a willing partnership in making Christ known.
But the greatest value of participating is not a discount or a product.
It is knowing that your voluntary support can help sustain work intended to point people toward Jesus.
Those free resources matter because biblical nourishment should not be reserved only for people who can pay.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Let it examine you.
Let it challenge the way you use your words.
Let it change the way you treat people who depend on you.
Let it remind you that the fear of God must be greater than the fear of losing face.
Let it teach you that courage sometimes means admitting that you were wrong.
And above all, let it lead you to Jesus.
Because the King of kings is not another Saul.
He is perfectly righteous.
He is never careless with His words.
He never confuses pride with holiness.
He does not need to defend a foolish decision.
He never has to repent of wrongdoing.
And when He calls sinners to Himself, He does not offer cheap reassurance that their sins do not matter.
He offers the forgiveness purchased by His own blood.
The Son of God was not spared the cross.
He willingly endured it.
And the empty tomb declares that death did not have the final word.
That is the Gospel.
That is our hope.
That is why we continue telling these stories.
Not because every biblical character is a hero.
Not because every painful situation ends the way we want.
But because all Scripture ultimately belongs to the greater story of God's redemptive purpose fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
Jonathan tasted honey and lived.
Jesus tasted death and rose again.
And through Him, sinners who deserve judgment can receive mercy, forgiveness, and new life.
What have I been defending that God is calling me to surrender?
Perhaps it is your pride.
Perhaps it is your bitterness.
Perhaps it is a secret sin.
Perhaps it is the need to control someone else.
Perhaps it is the lie that you are beyond forgiveness.
Bring it to Christ.
Do not wait until your heart feels ready to be honest.
Come into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Forgive where God calls you to forgive.
Make things right where you can.
And keep your eyes on the Savior whose grace does not merely cover the guilt of His people but also teaches them to live transformed lives.

The most heartbreaking part of Jonathan's story is that his father nearly took his life over a little honey. The most breathtaking truth of the Gospel is that Jesus willingly gave His life to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Never mistake the voice that wounded you for the voice of the Savior who died to redeem you.
